articles.title: White paper sets out blueprint for keeping innovation in the UK
articles.description: White paper sets out blueprint for keeping innovation in the UK Sarah Fell Wed, 10/21/2026 - 10:36 In Should I stay or should I go? A Pragmatic Path to Keeping UK Innovation at Home, Pascal Levensohn (founder of Levensohn Venture Partners LLC, Executive Chairman of Dolby Family Ventures, Chair of the Cambridge Innovation Hub Global Advisory Board and Fellow of Cambridge Judge Business School) says such a commitment can be implemented without difficult and time-consuming legislation. He argues that the debate over world-beating firms leaving the UK has conflated two separate questions – the health of the UK’s capital markets and the robustness of its innovation ecosystem – and has therefore misdiagnosed the problem. The commercial, rather than legislative, solution he proposes is a practical approach that can keep investment and high-quality jobs in the UK while the larger capital-markets debate proceeds. Foreign ownership is not the problem “Foreign acquisition is not the problem – and neither is foreign ownership,” says Levensohn. “A central problem is the failure to distinguish between three different forms of migration – of ownership and financial returns, of domicile and listing venue, and of productive capability. “Treated as a single, inevitable sequence, they obscure the opportunities for targeted intervention and invite the assumption that the first or second must lead to the third. It is the third that constitutes the avoidable national loss: a listing or an acquisition followed by the migration or erosion of substantive UK productive capability.” The solution he proposes in the paper is that: “The UK – government, universities, founders and the investment community together – should far more forcefully seek commitments from international investors and acquirers to create jobs and maintain a meaningful UK footprint for companies born in the UK, nourished by UK taxpayer investment, and first taking root in UK soil. The fruits from the UK’s innovation orchard can be harvested – ownership can change, returns can flow abroad – without pulling up the tree.” The paper quantifies what is at stake. Between 2015 and 2025, on average 40 UK deep-tech companies were acquired each year. If just 20 of them negotiated a binding commitment resulting in 25 net new UK-based jobs, sustained for the five-year life of the commitment, the programme would generate £312.5 million of additional gross value added a year by the fifth year and would cumulate to £2.5 billion over ten years. Levensohn cites precedents showing the feasibility of the approach, including the undertakings Japan’s SoftBank gave when it acquired Cambridge-based chip designer Arm in 2016 – to at least double Arm’s UK headcount within five years and keep its global headquarters in Cambridge – which the Takeover Panel’s independent supervisor later verified were honoured. Arm’s subsequent 2023 Nasdaq listing illustrates that a change of listing venue is not, in itself, the loss of UK productive capability. The paper ends with a call to action for UK leaders to convene a small, authoritative task force – drawing on founders, UK and international investors, strategic acquirers, M&A counsel, universities, public-policy experts and innovation clusters – with one mandate: to turn footprint retention into standard market practice. “The UK can continue to celebrate the companies it creates after their jobs, laboratories, compute, and manufacturing capacity have moved elsewhere. Or it can make retention a condition of serious stewardship: a standard board question, a standard investor expectation, and a standard term of doing business with the country’s most promising technologies. The UK does not need to close itself to global capital to keep more of what it creates. It needs to ask earlier, draft better, measure honestly, and then insist that the roots remain.” Adapted from an article first published by Cambridge Judge Business School. “Too many businesses are born in Britain but build their futures elsewhere. We should welcome global capital and negotiate harder to keep research, skills and high-value jobs at home. This timely whitepaper offers a practical way to do both.” Professor Gishan Dissanaike, Dean of Cambridge Judge Business School Yes

articles.title: Under-Skin Implant Controls Prosthetic Arms
articles.description: Two patients in Melbourne, Australia recently became the first recipients of a novel type of implant for controlling prosthetic arms. The 2-by-10-centimenter device, produced by Phantom Neuro, wraps around the forearm underneath the skin, where it measures electrical signals in muscles, a process called electromyography (EMG). That signal is then processed and translated into robotic commands for third-party prostheses. Options to control powered prosthetic devices that are currently available or in development look for signals from the brain, peripheral nerves, or muscles. Some methods also use a form of EMG, but inject probes deep into muscle. Surgeries to implant brain-based sensors can be even more invasive. Non-invasive approaches are commonly used, but often have their own drawbacks in reliability, comfort, or convenience. “The goal with this tech is to give amazing control, but with outpatient [care] more like a cosmetic procedure than brain surgery,” says Connor Glass, founder and CEO of Phantom Neuro, which is based in Austin, Texas. He describes the surgery as creating a pocket under the skin, comparable to common cosmetic implant procedures. Removal, when needed, is expected to be simpler than implantation. The company announced the successful procedures today, 20 October, about five months after the first took place. This is the first progress announced in an early feasibility trial in humans to assess the implant’s safety, which was approved by Australian regulators in April. A promising first procedure Michael Easy, a 32-year-old carpenter from Hastings, Victoria, near Melbourne, was the first implant recipient. “It was a bit sore and tender for the first couple of days and then it healed so quick, there was no drama whatsoever,” he says in statements relayed by Phantom Neuro. Easy also reports he experienced some swelling for two weeks post-operation. Easy was under operation for around an hour with mild sedation, and the entire process took about four hours. The second participant’s procedure was faster: It took around 45 minutes, notably did not use general anesthesia, and had the patient in and out of the hospital in three hours. Neural implant procedures can take many hours. The Phantom implant includes two rows of electrodes embedded in flexible medical silicone, with a disk of electronics at one end to process and send a wireless signal. A coil in the center is used for power delivery from an external source, similar to how a cochlear implant is powered. What works for one or two patients may not work for everyone, but aspects of early performance have been promising. For example, muscle signals have been strong and consistent, says Glass, and calibration between intent and gesture may last months, compared to the daily recalibration required with some surface EMG. “This implant has made everything easier and smoother and faster,” says Easy. Prosthesis control experts saw promise in the concept and form factor, but hoped for more public technical information and emphasized that at such an early stage of clinical research, many aspects of the device remain to be proven. “I see a tremendous potential benefit for patients to use every day more reliably,” says Helen Huang, a biomedical engineer at North Carolina State University. “Ultimately, these potential advantages must translate into tangible benefits for users, including more natural and reliable prosthetic control, reduced effort, and improved performance in daily activities,” says Loredana Zollo, a biomedical engineer at the Università Campus Bio-Medico di Roma. Why Phantom Neuro goes under the skin’s surface Costs and benefits will in part be compared to the relatively common surface EMG approach. Surface electrodes sit on top of the skin and can be finicky when placed slightly off the target location, and the user’s sweat can change the impedance or cause them to shift on the skin. They may be uncomfortable as they dig into skin, and motion tends to create data artifacts. All of these issues can be made worse by physical activity. Phantom Neuro’s under-the-skin approach offers a potentially more reliable alternative, but presents its own engineering challenges, says Glass. The implant must be able to withstand minor impacts from daily activity and maintain connection with an external power source despite movement of the arm and skin. The company also designed it to be compatible with a wide range of commercially-available prostheses, which do not have standardized communication protocols. Phantom’s current implants use machine learning to associate muscle signals with specific gestures or movements, and can perform the same action at different speeds. But the implant cannot yet combine motions, such as wrist rotation and finger movement, and requires step-by-step motions to achieve some tasks. A long-term goal is to use more sophisticated pattern recognition to achieve what Glass calls “simultaneous proportional control.” Glass is hopeful that in two to three years, clinical trial progression will lead to FDA approval for upper limb prosthesis control, after which the company may pursue other commercial applications or patient groups. Phantom is already starting to look into some of these, including medical applications in lower limb prostheses, which are particularly challenging. (No commercial systems that use EMG are yet available.) Phantom is also exploring general augmentation and human-machine interactions in defense settings.
